hero.title: The Foundation of The Laser Working أسس عمل الليزر
hero.lead: Three physical processes are of great importance to the physical foundations of laser generation: induced absorption, spontaneous emission, and stimulated emission — leading up to the concept of population inversion, which makes laser action possible.

objectives: Explain the process of induced absorption and the condition for an atom's transition between two energy levels.
Distinguish between spontaneous emission and stimulated emission in terms of mechanism and the properties of the resulting photons.
Explain the concept of population inversion and its importance in achieving laser action.

content.heading: 💡 6-3 The Foundation of The Laser Working أسس عمل الليزر
content.html: There are three processes of great importance to the physical foundations of laser generation: (induced absorption, spontaneous emission, stimulated emission).

content.label: 📌 Definition — Symbols of the energy transition law
content.html:
📌 Definition — Symbols of the energy transition law
  • \( h \) — Planck's constant, equal to (\(6.63\times10^{-34}\ \text{J.s}\)) joule·second
  • \( f \) — the frequency of the incident light, in hertz (Hz)
  • \( E_2, E_1 \) — the energy levels, in electron-volts (eV)

content.label: 📌 1- Induced Absorption Induced Absorption
content.html: This is the transition of an atom from a low energy level (\(E_1\)) to an excited energy level (\(E_2\)), by absorbing a photon whose energy equals the energy difference between these two levels, i.e., \( hf = E_2 - E_1 \). See Figure 6-6.

content.label: 📌 2- Spontaneous Emission Spontaneous Emission
content.html: When an atom is in a higher energy level (the excited level), it always tends toward a stable state, so it returns spontaneously — after a short time interval called the lifetime of the excited level — to the ground level. This transition is accompanied by the emission of a photon whose energy equals the energy difference between the two levels: \( hf = E_2 - E_1 \) (this transition is called spontaneous emission). content.html: The lifetime of a level: this is a very short time interval that an electron may spend in the higher energy level to which it transitions within an excited atom.

content.label: 📌 3- Stimulated Emission Stimulated Emission
content.html: When a photon collides with an atom in the excited level (\(E_2\)) such that its energy exactly equals the energy difference between the two levels (\(E_2-E_1\)), it will stimulate the atom to transition from level (\(E_2\)) to the lower level (\(E_1\)), resulting in the emission of a new photon identical (in energy, frequency, phase, and direction) to the photon that struck the atom (this type of transition is called stimulated emission). content.html: To obtain stimulated emission, spontaneous emission must occur first.

content.heading: 🔄 Thermal Equilibrium and Population Inversion
content.html: Under standard conditions (a state of thermal equilibrium) for any substance, most atoms are in the low energy levels, and only a smaller fraction of atoms are excited into the higher energy levels. See Figure 6-10.

To increase the probability of stimulated emission, the number of excited atoms in the higher energy levels must be greater than the number of atoms in the lower energy levels — that is, the distribution of atoms must be inverted; this process is therefore called (population inversion).

content.label: 📌 Definition — Population Inversion (Population Inversion)
content.html: This is the state in which the number of atoms in the higher energy level is greater than their number in the lower energy level, contrary to ordinary thermal equilibrium — and it is the necessary condition for achieving stimulated emission and generating laser light.

content.sectionHeading: 🕹️ Interactive simulation: The three fundamental processes
content.descriptionHtml: Choose a process to watch the atom and photons move between the energy levels E₁ and E₂.

labels.captionDefault: Click one of the buttons above to watch the process.
labels.captionAbsorption: An incoming photon strikes the atom in the ground level E₁, which absorbs its energy and transitions to the excited level E₂.
labels.captionSpontaneous: The atom in the excited level E₂ returns spontaneously, after the level's lifetime, to E₁, emitting a photon of random direction.
labels.captionStimulated: An incident photon stimulates the atom present in E₂, causing it to transition to E₁, producing a new photon identical to the incident one in energy, phase, and direction.

questions.question: The transition of an atom from a low level to an excited level by absorbing a photon is called:
questions.explain: Induced absorption is the transition of an atom from a low level E₁ to an excited level E₂ by absorbing a photon of energy hf=E₂-E₁.

questions.question: The photons produced by spontaneous emission are:
questions.explain: Photons from spontaneous emission differ in phase and direction, so they are emitted in every direction, like ordinary light.

questions.question: The condition necessary for stimulated emission to occur is:
options: The absence of any incoming photon
The atom being in the ground level
A photon whose energy equals the energy difference between the two levels striking an atom in the excited level
questions.explain: Stimulated emission occurs when a photon whose energy equals (E₂-E₁) strikes an atom in the excited level, producing a new photon exactly identical to the incident photon.

questions.question: Under standard thermal equilibrium conditions, most of a substance's atoms are distributed in:
options: An equal distribution among all levels
questions.explain: Under thermal equilibrium, most atoms are in the lower energy levels, with only a smaller fraction in the higher levels.

questions.question: The state in which the number of excited atoms in the higher levels exceeds their number in the lower levels is called:
questions.explain: Population inversion is the state in which the number of excited atoms exceeds the number of atoms in the lower levels, and it is a necessary condition for achieving stimulated emission.

summary.heading: 📋 Lesson Summary
items: The energy transition law between two levels: \(hf=E_2-E_1\), where h is Planck's constant (\(6.63\times10^{-34}\ \text{J.s}\)).
Induced absorption: a transition from E₁ to E₂ by absorbing a photon. Spontaneous emission: a random return from E₂ to E₁ after the level's lifetime.
Stimulated emission: an incident photon of energy (E₂-E₁) stimulates an excited atom, producing a new, exactly identical photon — the basis of laser operation.
Population inversion: the number of atoms in the higher level exceeds their number in the lower level, contrary to ordinary thermal equilibrium — the necessary condition for generating laser light.
